# Steam reaction toy (aeolipile) (`steam_aeolipile`)

<!-- generated by scripts/build_techtree.py from techtree/core/energy.yaml — do not edit -->

- Category: Energy & engines (`energy`)
- Core idea: A closed hollow ball on a hollow axle, with two bent nozzles pointing opposite ways, spins when steam from a boiling cauldron below is fed into it. It shows that steam can make motion. It is a simple reaction turbine. The ball can spin rapidly under a light load, but torque is small, steam leaks at the pivots and the exhaust carries energy away. Hero describes no practical machine driven by it. The road to a useful engine does not start here but with the piston and the vacuum left by condensing steam.
- Pitfalls:
  - Claiming the ancients nearly had the steam engine; nothing connects the aeolipile to the piston engine
  - Trying to scale it up to drive machinery; a jet engine only pays at speeds and pressures out of reach before the 1880s
  - A sealed vessel on a fire with nozzles that can block; it becomes a bomb
- History: rome: c. 25 BC – Vitruvius (I.6) mentions aeolipilae, bronze vessels that blow steam, as a model for the winds; greece: 1st c. AD – Hero of Alexandria describes the spinning ball in the Pneumatica; islamic: 1551 – Taqi al-Din in Damascus describes a steam jet turning a roasting spit; europe: 1629 – Giovanni Branca pictures a steam jet driving a paddle wheel and stamps; never built to useful size
- Read:
  - Hero of Alexandria, Pneumatica (tr. Bennet Woodcroft, 1851)
  - J. G. Landels, Engineering in the Ancient World (1978)
